title: Distributed Systems
description: Kafka/RabbitMQ, sharding, replication, CAP, consensus, LB, service discovery, SAML SSO. Turing FDE Stage 4 system design + Stage 1 MCQ.

questions.prompt: In CAP, during a network partition a system MUST sacrifice:
questions.explanation: During a partition you MUST pick C or A. Partition tolerance is non-negotiable in real distributed systems. PACELC extends: Else (no partition) → trade Latency vs Consistency.

questions.prompt: Which is TRUE about eventual consistency?

options.text: Writes propagate asynchronously; reads may return stale data, but replicas converge given no new writes

questions.explanation: AP systems (DynamoDB default, Cassandra) trade freshness for availability. Read-your-writes / monotonic reads are sub-guarantees you can layer on.

questions.prompt: Kafka partitions guarantee ordering:

options.text: Within a single partition only — use a partition key on messages that must be ordered relative to each other

questions.explanation: Pick a good key (e.g., customer_id) so all events for one entity land on one partition. Trade-off: hot keys create hot partitions.

questions.prompt: Which are TRUE about Kafka consumer groups? (select all)

options.text: Within a group, each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer
Adding more consumers than partitions leaves some idle
Different groups can independently consume the same topic
Consumers auto-commit offsets by default (potential double-processing on crash)

questions.explanation: Parallelism ceiling = # partitions. Auto-commit is convenient but at-least-once semantics require idempotent processing.

questions.prompt: When would you pick RabbitMQ over Kafka?

options.text: You need durable, replayable log with high throughput
Complex routing (topic/fanout/headers exchanges), per-message ack, low-latency work-queue semantics; smaller throughput

questions.explanation: RabbitMQ is a smart broker (routing) with per-message ack. Kafka is a distributed log with dumb-broker + smart-consumer. Different tools.

questions.prompt: Exactly-once delivery in a distributed system is:

options.text: Achievable end-to-end only via idempotent consumers (dedup by message id) OR transactional writes (Kafka EOS + transactional producer)

questions.explanation: Two Generals means true exactly-once at network level is impossible. In practice: at-least-once + idempotent processing OR EOS with transactions.

questions.prompt: You shard user data by `user_id % N`. Adding a shard requires:

options.text: Rehashing most of the data — huge migration. Use consistent hashing instead to minimize movement

questions.explanation: Modulo hashing fails to scale. Consistent hashing moves ~1/N of keys when adding a shard. Vitess/Cassandra use variants of this.

questions.prompt: Cross-shard queries (e.g., 'top spenders across all shards') are typically handled by:

options.text: Scatter-gather to all shards + aggregation node OR a separate analytics store (warehouse / CDC-fed)

questions.explanation: Scatter-gather at OLTP scale is expensive. Most systems replicate to a warehouse for analytics.

questions.prompt: Postgres streaming replication is 'async by default'. Failing over immediately after a write may:

options.text: Lose the last few in-flight writes (RPO > 0)

questions.explanation: Async = write ack before replica catches up. Use synchronous_commit=on with a synchronous_standby_names for RPO=0 at latency cost.

questions.prompt: Raft's key correctness property:

options.text: Any two nodes see the same log
In any elected term there is at most one leader; committed entries survive across leader changes

questions.explanation: Leader election + log matching + safety properties. Used in etcd, Consul, CockroachDB.

questions.prompt: Sticky sessions are needed when:

options.text: The app holds session state in-memory per-node (WebSocket connection, unshared cache, etc.)

questions.explanation: Stateless apps + shared session store (Redis) removes the need for stickiness — recommended pattern.

questions.prompt: Which LB algorithm balances best when backend request cost varies wildly?
questions.explanation: RR ignores load. Least-connections sends new requests to the least-loaded backend, evening out variable-cost work.

questions.prompt: Circuit-breaker's 'half-open' state does:

options.text: Sends a limited probe request; success closes the circuit, failure re-opens it

questions.explanation: 3-state pattern (closed → open → half-open) prevents thundering-herd on recovery.

questions.prompt: In a Kafka→Flink pipeline where Flink can't keep up:

options.text: Flink buffers fill; Flink stops fetching → Kafka lag grows; alert on lag + scale Flink or throttle producers

questions.explanation: Backpressure propagates upstream. Alert on consumer-lag; scale downstream or shed load.

questions.prompt: The Saga pattern is:

options.text: A sequence of local transactions across services with compensating actions on failure (eventual consistency)

questions.explanation: Choreography (events) or orchestration (central coordinator). Compensations undo prior steps rather than rolling back.

questions.prompt: The Transactional Outbox pattern solves:

options.text: Reliably publishing an event AFTER the DB commit — write both to DB + outbox table in one txn; separate poller/CDC publishes

questions.explanation: Prevents 'wrote to DB but message never sent' and vice versa. Debezium reads the outbox via CDC to Kafka.

questions.prompt: Change Data Capture (CDC) via Debezium reads:

options.text: The database's write-ahead log (WAL/binlog) as a stream of row changes → Kafka

questions.explanation: WAL/binlog = source of truth for every mutation; low overhead vs polling.

questions.prompt: Distributed lock via `SETNX` in Redis is unsafe when:

options.text: Client A's lock expires (GC pause) but A thinks it still holds it; B acquires; both write → conflict

questions.explanation: Classic Redlock critique (Martin Kleppmann). Use fencing tokens + optimistic checks or ZooKeeper for correctness-critical locks.

questions.prompt: In Kubernetes, service discovery for pod-to-pod calls typically uses:

options.text: Cluster DNS (kube-dns/CoreDNS) resolving `service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local` to a stable ClusterIP

questions.explanation: Service abstracts pod IPs. Headless services (clusterIP: None) return the pod IPs directly for client-side LB.

questions.prompt: Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) propagates context between services via:

options.text: HTTP headers (traceparent / tracestate) or messaging metadata carrying trace_id + span_id

questions.explanation: W3C Trace Context standard. Auto-instrumentation libs inject/extract on HTTP/gRPC/Kafka clients.

questions.prompt: An SLO of 99.9% availability over 30 days gives you an error budget of:
Active-active multi-region with a single logical DB is hard because:

options.text: Write consistency across regions requires either global consensus (latency) or conflict resolution (CRDTs / last-writer-wins with tradeoffs)

questions.explanation: Options: Spanner/CockroachDB (global consensus, latency cost), per-region writes with async replication (conflict handling), or route users to a home region.

questions.prompt: Cache-aside (lazy-loading) vs write-through — cache-aside's typical downside:

options.text: First read is a cache miss; stale cache after DB update unless explicitly invalidated

questions.explanation: Write-through keeps cache in sync but adds write latency. Cache-aside with TTL is the common default.

questions.prompt: Choose queue tech: 'we need at-least-once delivery, per-key ordering, replay, 100k msg/sec'.

options.text: Kafka — partition-key ordering, replay from offsets, high throughput

questions.explanation: SQS FIFO caps at 3000 msg/s/queue (batched). RabbitMQ lacks replay. Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget.

questions.prompt: The 'distributed monolith' anti-pattern is:

options.text: Microservices that must be deployed together, share a DB, and have synchronous fan-out chains — worst of both worlds

questions.explanation: Symptoms: shared DB, chatty RPCs, coordinated releases, cascading failures. Fix by decoupling boundaries + async messaging.

questions.prompt: Which are core resilience patterns? (select all)
questions.explanation: Netflix Hystrix / Resilience4j / Polly ship all four. Global mutex reduces resilience.

questions.prompt: Gossip protocols (Cassandra, Consul membership) trade:

options.text: Instant convergence for gradual, eventually-consistent state spread — highly available, no single point of failure

questions.explanation: Peers randomly exchange state → epidemic spread → converges in O(log N).

questions.prompt: Simple leader election via 'lowest node ID wins' fails when:

options.text: Network partition means each side elects a leader → split brain; requires quorum-based election (Raft/ZooKeeper)

questions.explanation: Quorum (majority) prevents two leaders from being validly elected simultaneously.

questions.prompt: The 'four golden signals' (Google SRE) are:
questions.explanation: Foundational SRE metric set for any service dashboard.

questions.prompt: The idempotency key pattern requires:

options.text: Client generates a unique key per LOGICAL operation; server stores and returns the same result on retries with that key

questions.explanation: Stripe/Square-style. Store result keyed by (idempotency_key, endpoint) with TTL. Handles retries + network duplicates cleanly.
